questions.prompt: The previous level covered precise, Thomistic terms -- prudence as 'charioteer of the virtues,' the connexio virtutum. Someone assumes 'charioteer' actually means prudence alone matters, and the other cardinal virtues are actually optional extras. What is the real, precise correction?
choices: 'Charioteer' means prudence actively directs the other cardinal virtues toward good -- it doesn't make them optional
This real, assumption is actually correct -- prudence alone actually matters, and justice, fortitude, and temperance are actually optional
'Charioteer' actually has no real, precise, technical meaning at all, and can be genuinely used however a person likes
'Charioteer' actually means prudence should actually be abandoned in favor of the other three, real, cardinal virtues
questions.correctAnswer: 'Charioteer' means prudence actively directs the other cardinal virtues toward good -- it doesn't make them optional
questions.explanation: This is a real, precise, important correction -- 'charioteer' means prudence actively directs and guides the other cardinal virtues toward the good, not that they're genuinely optional; a charioteer still needs real horses to actually drive.
questions.hint: Recall the previous level's own real definition of prudence as the 'charioteer' guiding the other virtues.

questions.prompt: Someone deliberately takes an unnecessary physical risk, saying they're doing it 'for God' and trusting He'll protect them. Using the fortitude/audacia (rashness) distinction, how should this be evaluated?
choices: This more closely resembles audacia (rashness) than true fortitude, since real courage requires facing a genuinely necessary danger for a right reason, not manufacturing unnecessary risk
This is automatically true fortitude, since any risk taken while invoking God's name is virtuous by definition
Fortitude and audacia are simply two names for the same virtue
True fortitude requires seeking out the greatest possible danger available in any situation
questions.correctAnswer: This more closely resembles audacia (rashness) than true fortitude, since real courage requires facing a genuinely necessary danger for a right reason, not manufacturing unnecessary risk
questions.explanation: True fortitude, per ST II-II q.123, faces real, necessary danger for a genuinely good end, guided by prudence about when facing danger is actually called for. Manufacturing unnecessary risk and simply trusting divine protection to justify it looks much more like audacia -- rashness -- than genuine courage, which doesn't seek danger for its own sake.
questions.hint: Real fortitude requires the danger to actually be necessary for a good end, not invented.

citations.quote: Fortitude is the moral virtue that ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good.

questions.prompt: A manager avoids reporting a colleague's serious ethical violation, reasoning that staying quiet protects their own career and keeps the peace. Is this genuine prudence?
choices: No -- this is closer to 'prudence of the flesh' (ST II-II q.55 a.1), where self-interested calculation is disguised as practical wisdom rather than actually seeking the true good
Yes -- avoiding any workplace conflict is always the prudent choice
Yes -- prudence means always prioritizing one's own career above other considerations
This scenario has nothing to do with the virtue of prudence at all
questions.correctAnswer: No -- this is closer to 'prudence of the flesh' (ST II-II q.55 a.1), where self-interested calculation is disguised as practical wisdom rather than actually seeking the true good
questions.explanation: 'Prudence of the flesh' names a counterfeit: using genuine practical reasoning skill in service of self-interest rather than the true good, dressing up self-protective calculation as wisdom. Real prudence orders action toward what is actually good, even when that requires real personal cost.
questions.hint: The counterfeit uses real reasoning skill, just aimed at the wrong target -- self-protection instead of the true good.

citations.quote: Prudence is the virtue that disposes practical reason to discern our true good in every circumstance and to choose the right means of achieving it.

questions.prompt: True or False: Someone who says, 'God will save me no matter what I do, so my choices don't really matter,' is expressing the theological virtue of hope in its proper, healthy form.
questions.explanation: CCC 2091-2092 names this presumption, a distortion of hope in one of two ways -- either presuming on one's own capacities without grace, or presuming on God's mercy without genuine conversion and cooperation. Genuine hope trusts God's help while still taking one's own free response and moral choices seriously, not treating them as irrelevant.
questions.hint: The Catechism has a specific name for hope distorted into treating personal choices as no longer mattering.

citations.quote: Either man presumes upon his own capacities... or he presumes upon God's almighty power or his mercy (hoping to obtain his forgiveness without conversion and glory without merit).

questions.prompt: A person gives away money generously but does so without any judgment about real need, leaving their own family without necessities. Using the connexio virtutum, how should this be assessed?
choices: Despite real generosity, the lack of prudent judgment about competing real goods means this person is not yet fully virtuous -- the virtues are meant to work together, not in isolation
This person has achieved perfect virtue, since generosity alone is sufficient for virtue
Prudence is irrelevant to acts of generosity
This shows generosity and prudence are actually the same virtue
questions.correctAnswer: Despite real generosity, the lack of prudent judgment about competing real goods means this person is not yet fully virtuous -- the virtues are meant to work together, not in isolation
questions.explanation: This is exactly what the connexio virtutum thesis predicts: a real virtue (generosity, related to justice/liberality) exercised without prudence's guidance about genuinely competing goods and obligations doesn't yet count as perfected virtue -- the virtues must work together, not operate as isolated, unconnected traits.
questions.hint: Look back to level 6's fortitude-without-prudence example -- this is the same principle applied to a different virtue.

citations.quote: The moral virtues grow through education, deliberate acts, and perseverance in struggle.

questions.prompt: An objector says, 'Faith is just an emotional comfort people use to feel better -- it isn't really a virtue at all.' What is the accurate response, drawing on this topic's definition of theological virtue?
choices: Faith is a real, infused disposition of the intellect and will assenting to revealed truth on God's authority, not merely a feeling of comfort, even though genuine faith may or may not be accompanied by comforting feelings
The Church agrees faith is nothing more than an emotional coping mechanism
Faith requires the total absence of any doubt or difficult feeling to be genuine
Feelings of comfort are what actually define and constitute genuine faith
questions.correctAnswer: Faith is a real, infused disposition of the intellect and will assenting to revealed truth on God's authority, not merely a feeling of comfort, even though genuine faith may or may not be accompanied by comforting feelings
questions.explanation: As level 6 established, theological virtue is a real, infused disposition of intellect and will, not reducible to an emotional state -- faith can coexist with real doubt, dryness, or difficulty, since it is an assent of intellect and will to God's revealed truth on his authority, not a guaranteed emotional payoff.
questions.hint: Look back to level 6's definition of theological virtue -- an emotional feeling was never part of that definition.

citations.quote: Faith is the theological virtue by which we believe in God and believe all that he has said and revealed to us... because he is truth itself.

questions.prompt: Match each counterfeit or distortion to the genuine virtue it imitates falsely.

pairs.right: True fortitude, which faces only genuinely necessary danger for a right reason
True prudence, which seeks the actual good rather than self-interest disguised as wisdom
True hope, which trusts God's help while still taking one's own free response seriously

pairs.left: False modesty denying a real accomplishment
pairs.right: True magnanimity, which honestly acknowledges real gifts ordered toward good ends

questions.explanation: Each of these counterfeits borrows the appearance of a real virtue while missing something essential -- right reason, the true good, genuine cooperation, or plain honesty -- that the authentic virtue actually requires.
questions.hint: Every 'false' version in the left column looks similar to its true counterpart on the surface, but is missing one key ingredient.

citations.quote: Fortitude is the moral virtue that ensures firmness in difficulties and constancy in the pursuit of the good.

questions.prompt: A person insists on total self-sufficiency, refusing all help even when genuinely needed, calling it 'strength.' What does this most resemble?
choices: A counterfeit of fortitude — true fortitude includes the humility to accept help when needed, not an isolating refusal that is closer to pride
Genuine fortitude in its purest form
The theological virtue of hope
A form of prudence
questions.correctAnswer: A counterfeit of fortitude — true fortitude includes the humility to accept help when needed, not an isolating refusal that is closer to pride
questions.explanation: Fortitude is firmness in pursuit of a real good, not an aversion to depending on anyone. Refusing help out of a need to appear invulnerable is usually pride wearing fortitude's clothing, and the connexio virtutum thesis explains why: real fortitude cannot be severed from humility and prudence.
questions.hint: Ask whether accepting help when it is genuinely needed is a failure of courage or an exercise of it.

questions.prompt: Someone treats every rule as negotiable 'for a greater good' they alone determine, overriding clear obligations whenever it suits their judgment. What is this a distortion of?
choices: Prudence — genuine prudence submits itself to real moral principles rather than using 'discernment' to override them at will
Charity, properly understood
Justice, in its fullest sense
Fortitude, exercised rightly
questions.correctAnswer: Prudence — genuine prudence submits itself to real moral principles rather than using 'discernment' to override them at will
questions.explanation: Prudence applies principles wisely to particular cases; it does not manufacture exceptions to principles whenever convenient. A 'prudence' that always concludes in favor of what the person already wanted has stopped being prudence and become a cover for the will.
questions.hint: Ask whether real discernment can ever conclude the opposite of what someone wanted to do.

questions.prompt: True or False: Genuine humility means believing you have no talents or gifts worth anything.
questions.explanation: False. That is a counterfeit — false modesty, which can itself be a subtle form of pride, refusing gifts God actually gave. Real humility is accurate self-knowledge: seeing both one's real gifts and real limits truthfully, and referring the gifts back to their giver rather than denying them exist.
questions.hint: Ask whether denying a real gift is honesty, or a different kind of self-focus.
